evals.prompt: I want to add a new `explain` subcommand to the qoq CLI. It should read the last gate run's report from `.qoq/` (written by `gate`, see references/gate.md's verdict format) and print a human-readable summary — what was auto-applied, what advisories remain — instead of making someone read the raw JSON. Can you plan this out before we start building it? Don't start implementing yet, just get me the plan.
evals.expected_output: A plan file under ./plans/ (or an equivalent workspace output path for this test run) following the planning-gate template: goal/architecture/requirements-source header, at least one milestone with tickets sized XS-M, each ticket complexity-rated and tiered, files listed as exact paths within packages/cli (discovered from the real repo, not invented), a testing-gate + qoq gate step in each ticket's definition of done, and a milestone-level qoq gate + full build/test phase. No placeholder text.
assertions: A plan markdown file exists at the specified output path and is non-empty.
The plan file includes the required header fields: Goal, Architecture, Requirements source, and Plan status.
At least one Milestone is present with a Size field (S/M/L/XL) and at least one Ticket.

Every ticket has non-blank Status, Size, Complexity, and Agent tier fields, and the Agent tier assigned is consistent with the Complexity rating (a trivial/mechanical ticket gets a cheap tier; a judgment-heavy ticket is tiered at the session's own model, not at some named model above it).
No ticket is sized larger than M — an L or XL ticket size anywhere in the plan is a failure, since oversized work is supposed to be split during decomposition.
Every ticket is assigned to a subagent tier — no ticket is left as 'main-thread' or otherwise marked for the orchestrator to implement itself.
Every ticket carries an Escalation field, set to 'none' on a freshly drafted plan.

Every ticket's Definition of done includes a qoq gate step naming that ticket's own files, and includes a testing-gate step if and only if that ticket's Files field lists a test file to create or modify.
The milestone-level Definition of done includes a qoq gate run with no explicit paths plus the project's full build/test commands (not the scoped single-file commands).
The milestone-level Definition of done includes archiving the delivered milestone to a companion .completed.md file, leaving a summary block in the plan.
Ticket Files fields reference plausible real paths under packages/cli discovered from the actual qoq repo, not generic/invented paths like 'src/index.ts'.
The plan contains no unresolved placeholder text (e.g. 'TBD', 'similar to Ticket X', 'handle edge cases', 'etc.').
Before decomposing, the transcript shows a setup check confirming that qoq is available/installed.
Repository discovery was delegated to an Explore (or equivalent) subagent rather than the main thread grepping the codebase itself.

evals.prompt: here's the ask from product: users should be able to reset their password via an email link. token should expire in 1 hour. we don't have any email sending set up in this app yet so we'd probably need to add something like nodemailer or similar. can you turn this into tickets for the team? this is for the sample-nest-app project.
evals.expected_output: A plan file decomposing password-reset-via-email into sized, complexity-rated, tiered tickets grounded in the fixture project's actual UsersService/UsersController shape (discovered, not invented). The new email-sending dependency is flagged under a ticket's 'Needs approval' field rather than silently added to package.json. Each ticket has a testing-gate + qoq gate step; a milestone-level full quality suite phase is present.
assertions: A plan markdown file exists in the outputs directory and is non-empty.

At least one ticket has a Needs approval field (or clearly equivalent flag) naming the new email-sending dependency (e.g. nodemailer) as needing user approval, rather than the plan silently assuming it's already installed.
The new dependency is also surfaced to the user at plan-approval time, not left only inside the ticket body.
The fixture project's package.json was not modified — the new dependency was flagged, not installed (git diff/status in the project directory shows no change to package.json).

Ticket Files fields reference the actual existing files discovered in the fixture (src/users/users.service.ts and/or src/users/users.controller.ts), not invented paths unrelated to the real project structure.
Every ticket has non-blank Status, Size, Complexity, and Agent tier fields, and no ticket is sized larger than M.

Every ticket's Definition of done includes a qoq gate step, and includes a testing-gate step only on tickets whose Files field lists a test file; the milestone-level definition of done includes a full-suite qoq gate plus the project's own build/test commands.
The plan contains no unresolved placeholder text.

evals.prompt: We need to (1) add Stripe billing with subscription tiers, (2) redesign the settings page UI with a new tab layout, and (3) migrate our logging from console.log to a structured logger across the whole codebase. Give me one plan with milestones for all of this — I don't want three separate plan files, just put it all in one so I can track it in one place. This is for the sample-nest-app project.
evals.expected_output: The skill should push back on bundling three independent subsystems into a single plan (the scope check), explain why, and recommend/produce separate plans per subsystem instead of silently complying with 'one plan file' — rather than either refusing the request outright or complying without comment.
assertions: The response explicitly addresses why bundling Stripe billing, a settings UI redesign, and a logging migration into one plan is a problem (a scope-check style explanation), rather than silently complying with the 'one plan file' instruction or flatly refusing the whole request.

The final output results in multiple separate plan files (or a clear, explicit recommendation to split into separate plans, with at least one produced) rather than a single plan file covering all three subsystems with no comment.

Each resulting plan file that exists is well-formed against the template (has Goal/Architecture/Requirements source/Plan status, at least one milestone, at least one sized/complexity-rated/tiered ticket).
The plan(s) contain no unresolved placeholder text.

evals.prompt: plan out adding a `--json` output flag to the qoq CLI's gate command (so CI can parse the verdict instead of scraping stdout). don't build it yet. also before I let this loose on the codebase — walk me through how you'd actually dispatch these tickets, and what happens if the cheap agent you picked keeps failing the gate. I got burned last time by an agent that just kept retrying forever.
evals.expected_output: A plan file plus an explicit walkthrough of the execution model: every ticket dispatched to a subagent (nothing implemented by the orchestrator itself), each dispatch carrying a three-attempt delivery budget, and a failing subagent returning a 'This feels too complex for me' handoff report that causes re-dispatch one tier up — with the top tier failing meaning blocked-and-escalated-to-user, not silently absorbed by the main thread.
assertions: A well-formed plan markdown file exists (Goal/Architecture/Requirements source/Plan status header, at least one milestone, tickets with Status/Size/Complexity/Agent tier).
The response states that every ticket is executed by a dispatched subagent and that the orchestrator/main thread does not implement tickets itself.
The response names a bounded retry budget of exactly three delivery attempts (implement/fix + gate) per dispatch, rather than 'retry until it works' or an unspecified 'reasonable effort'.
The response describes the failing subagent reporting back with a handoff message beginning 'This feels too complex for me' (or quotes that exact signal phrase).
The response describes escalation as re-dispatching the same ticket to a stronger tier with the previous failure report included, not as the orchestrator taking the ticket over itself.
The response states that the escalation ladder stops at the model the user is already running the session on — the skill does not pick a more expensive model above that ceiling on the user's behalf.

The response describes passing the tier explicitly as the dispatch's model parameter (including for judgment-heavy tickets, where the session's own model ID is passed), rather than omitting the parameter and relying on inheritance.

The response states that a failure at the top tier results in the ticket being marked blocked and handed to the user to decide (respecify/split the ticket, or restart on a stronger model), rather than the main thread implementing it.
The response states that the gate is never loosened and the ticket scope is never narrowed to force a PASS.
The plan contains no unresolved placeholder text.

evals.prompt: resume ./plans/2026-07-20-audit-log.md — pick up where we left off.
evals.expected_output: The skill recognizes this as a resume: it reads the plan file fresh, skips tickets already marked done without re-gating them, does not re-run discovery or decomposition, and re-dispatches the blocked ticket at the tier recorded in its Escalation field (the tier it escalated TO), not the tier that already failed.
assertions: The transcript shows the plan file being read from disk at the start, rather than the skill working from an assumed or remembered plan.
Neither Phase 1 discovery nor Phase 2 decomposition is re-run: no Explore dispatch for repo discovery and no re-drafting of tickets that already exist in the plan.
Tickets already marked done are skipped — their gates are not re-run and their scope is not re-decided.
The blocked ticket whose Escalation field records a prior failed tier is re-dispatched at the tier it escalated TO, not at the tier that already failed.
The completed-milestones archive file is not read in full just to 'get up to speed' — the ## Completed summary block in the plan is treated as sufficient.
Work resumes in dependency order across the remaining todo/blocked tickets.

evals.prompt: All the tickets in Milestone 2 of ./plans/2026-07-20-audit-log.md are done now. Close the milestone out properly before we start Milestone 3.
evals.expected_output: The milestone gate runs (unscoped qoq gate plus the project's full build and test commands, not the scoped per-ticket commands), then the milestone is archived: its full text moves to the companion .completed.md file, a short summary block is left under ## Completed in the plan, and any fact established during delivery that a Milestone 2 ticket depends on is edited into that downstream ticket's Context field.
assertions: The milestone gate is run as unscoped `qoq gate` with no explicit paths, not a per-ticket scoped gate.
The project's full build and full test commands are run, not the scoped single-file variants a ticket gate would use.
The delivered milestone's full text is moved out of the plan file into the companion .completed.md file (appended, not overwriting existing archived milestones).

A short summary block for the milestone is left under a ## Completed section at the top of the plan, containing at minimum what was delivered, the tickets with their commits, and decisions that outlive the milestone.
The plan file is shorter after archiving than before — the milestone body is not duplicated in both files.

Ticket 3.1's Context is corrected to call `findByCaseId(caseId, page)` — the name Milestone 2 actually shipped, per Ticket 2.3's advisory — rather than the `findByCase` it was drafted against; recording that only in the ## Completed summary is a failure, since no subagent reads it.
If the milestone gate had failed, the failure would be written up as a new sized/rated/tiered ticket and dispatched — not patched on the main thread.
